questions.q: What is the recommended minimum concrete cover for reinforcing bars in footings or structural members in contact with the ground?
questions.n: The code requires a minimum of 75 mm of concrete cover when concrete is cast against and permanently exposed to earth.

questions.q: For a Class A concrete mix, what is the standard ratio of cement, sand, and gravel?
questions.n: Class A concrete follows a 1:2:4 volumetric proportion of cement to sand to gravel.

questions.q: Which structural member is specifically designed to resist bending and lateral loads simultaneously?
questions.n: A beam-column is a member subjected to both axial compression and transverse bending moments.

questions.q: What is the term for the failure of a column where it suddenly bows outward under an axial load?
questions.n: Buckling is the lateral deflection of a slender column when subjected to a critical axial load.

questions.q: According to ASTM standards, what is the diameter of a #3 reinforcing bar?
questions.n: Based on ASTM, a #3 bar is equivalent to a 10 mm diameter bar.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a slump test when performing quality control on concrete?
o: To check for initial setting time
To determine the consistency and workability
questions.n: The slump test is specifically used to determine the consistency of the concrete mix.

questions.q: In a simply supported beam, where is the maximum bending moment located when a uniform load is applied?
questions.n: For a uniformly distributed load, the maximum deflection and bending moment occur at the center of the span.

questions.q: Which local supplier is famously associated with steel products in the Philippines?
questions.n: Steel Asia is identified as a popular local supplier of steel.

questions.q: What is the purpose of adding a 'Retarder' admixture to a concrete mix?
o: To delay the initial setting of concrete
To reduce the amount of water needed
To speed up the curing process
questions.n: Retarders are substances added to alter the properties of concrete by delaying its setting time.

questions.q: Which foundation type is most suitable for supporting a structure on a site with a high water table and very deep bearing stratum?
questions.n: Piles transfer loads to deeper, more stable soil or rock layers, making them ideal for sites with poor surface soil or high water tables.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a tie beam in a foundation system?
o: To connect footings and resist differential settlement
To act as a retaining wall for the basement
To provide a base for the ground floor slab
To carry the vertical loads of the building
questions.n: Tie beams link individual footings to provide lateral stability and help the foundation act as a unit against uneven settlement.

questions.q: What happens to the strength of concrete if the water-cement ratio is significantly increased beyond the design mix?
questions.n: Excess water creates voids in the concrete as it evaporates, significantly reducing the final compressive strength.

questions.q: In structural steel, what is the 'web' of a Wide Flange (W-shape) section?
questions.n: The web is the vertical plate that connects the two flanges and primarily resists shear forces.

questions.q: What is the minimum diameter of reinforcing bars for stirrups in beams according to typical building codes?
questions.n: 10 mm is the standard minimum size for stirrups used to resist shear and hold longitudinal bars in place.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a 'Construction Joint' in concrete work?
o: The point where concrete pouring was stopped and continued later
A joint designed to allow for thermal expansion
The connection between steel and concrete
A crack that forms due to shrinkage
questions.n: Construction joints occur at locations where a pour is interrupted, requiring a surface for the next pour to bond to.

questions.q: What is the compressive strength of a Class B concrete mixture?
questions.n: A Class B concrete mix, with a ratio of 1:2.5:5, is typically rated at 2500 psi.

questions.q: In structural mechanics, what is 'Stress' defined as?
o: The change in length of a member
The total weight applied to a beam
The intensity of internal force per unit area
questions.n: Stress is the measure of internal resistance to an external load, calculated as Force divided by Area.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a 'Dowel' bar in concrete construction?
o: To act as a moisture barrier
To transfer stress from one concrete element to another
To provide aesthetic appeal to the surface
To replace the need for cement
questions.n: Dowels are short steel bars that bridge two concrete elements to transfer loads while allowing for some movement.

questions.q: Which material is known for being strong in compression but weak in tension?
questions.n: Concrete can withstand high crushing loads but requires steel reinforcement to handle pulling or stretching forces.

questions.q: What is the typical thickness of a 4-inch concrete slab expressed in metric units?
questions.n: Since 1 inch equals 25.4 mm, 4 inches is approximately 101.6 mm, commonly rounded to 100 mm.

questions.q: Which defect occurs when aggregate separates from the cement paste in concrete?
questions.n: Segregation is the separation of the constituents of a concrete mix, often caused by excessive vibration or dropping concrete from a height.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is 'Dwightsteel' primarily known for supplying?
o: Long span roofing and steel decking
questions.n: Dwightsteel is a major local supplier of roofing materials and structural steel floor decks.

questions.q: What structural element is designed to prevent a beam from sagging or 'camber' in the opposite direction?
questions.n: Cambering involves curving a beam slightly upward during manufacturing so that it levels out under its intended load.

questions.q: For a 10 cu.m. concrete pour using Class A mix, how many bags of cement (40kg) are required?
questions.n: Based on standard estimates, a Class A mix requires 9 bags per cubic meter, totaling 90 bags for 10 cu.m.

questions.q: What is the term for a beam that is supported at only one end?
questions.n: A cantilever is a beam fixed at one end and free at the other, common in balconies and canopies.

questions.q: What is 'Slenderness Ratio' used to determine in structural design?
o: The susceptibility of a column to buckling
questions.n: The slenderness ratio compares the length of a column to its cross-sectional dimensions to see how easily it will bow under load.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Stirrups' in a concrete beam?
o: To resist shear forces and hold longitudinal bars
To reduce the amount of sand needed
To prevent the beam from rusting
To increase the compressive strength of concrete
questions.n: Stirrups wrap around longitudinal bars to prevent them from moving and to resist diagonal tension (shear).

questions.q: Which foundation system is often called a 'Floating Foundation'?
questions.n: A mat foundation is a continuous slab that supports the entire structure, allowing it to 'float' on soil with low bearing capacity.

questions.q: What is the function of an 'Admixture' in concrete?
o: It is another name for the coarse aggregate
To serve as the primary binding agent
To replace the need for water
To modify the properties of fresh or hardened concrete
questions.n: Admixtures are chemicals or materials added to the mix to change things like setting time, workability, or durability.

questions.q: What is 'Curing' in the context of concrete work?
o: Removing the formwork immediately after pouring
Mixing the concrete for at least 30 minutes
Painting the concrete to make it look better
Maintaining moisture and temperature to ensure proper hydration
questions.n: Curing is the process of keeping concrete moist so the chemical reaction (hydration) can fully complete, maximizing strength.

questions.q: Which property of steel allows it to undergo significant deformation before breaking?
questions.n: Ductility is the ability of a material to deform plastically (stretch or bend) under tensile stress before failure.

questions.q: In a traverse calculation, if a line has a bearing of 'North to West', which quadrant is it in?
questions.n: A bearing from North toward the West is in the fourth quadrant, commonly called Northwest.

questions.q: What is the result of 'Honeycomb' in a concrete structural member?
o: It makes the concrete more lightweight
A decorative pattern on the surface
Voids or air pockets caused by poor vibration
questions.n: Honeycomb happens when the mortar fails to fill the spaces between coarse aggregates, often due to lack of vibration or congested steel.

questions.q: What is 'Strain' in a structural member?
o: The breaking point of the material
questions.n: Strain is a dimensionless measure of how much a material has stretched or compressed relative to its original size.

questions.q: What is the minimum concrete cover for reinforcing bars in a 'Slab on Fill'?
questions.n: Slabs on fill require a larger cover (50 mm) because they are in close proximity to ground moisture.

questions.q: Which type of joint is designed specifically to allow for independent movement between adjacent parts of a building?
questions.n: Expansion joints (and seismic gaps) allow for thermal expansion or seismic movement without causing damage to the whole structure.

questions.q: In structural design, what does 'Dead Load' refer to?
o: The weight of the building's own permanent components
The weight of the people in the building
The pressure from wind during a storm
The weight of snow on the roof
questions.n: Dead loads are the weights of permanent structures like slabs, beams, columns, walls, and fixed equipment.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Temperature Bars' in a concrete slab?
o: To make the concrete set faster
To support the weight of the furniture
To heat up the slab during winter
To resist cracks caused by expansion and contraction
questions.n: These bars help distribute stresses caused by changes in temperature and concrete shrinkage.

questions.q: What does a 'Slump Test' with a zero slump indicate?
o: The concrete mix is too dry
The concrete has too much sand
questions.n: A zero slump means the concrete did not settle at all when the cone was removed, indicating it lacks sufficient water for workability.

questions.q: Which steel section is commonly preferred for exposed architectural structures due to its clean aesthetic?
questions.n: Tubular sections have smooth surfaces and closed shapes that are visually appealing for exposed structural frames.

questions.q: What is the recommended minimum rebar size for a main column in a small residential building?
questions.n: 16 mm is a standard minimum size for longitudinal reinforcement in structural columns.

questions.q: Which foundation type consists of a long, reinforced concrete member driven into the ground?
questions.n: Piles are vertical structural elements driven or bored into the earth to reach deeper load-bearing strata.

questions.q: What is the compressive strength typically expected from a Class AA concrete mix?
questions.n: Class AA is a rich mix (1:1.5:3 ratio) designed to reach higher strengths, often around 4000 psi.

questions.q: In a structural drawing, what does 'NTS' usually stand for?
questions.n: NTS indicates that the drawing or detail is not drawn at a precise mathematical scale.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'Planted Column'?
o: A column made of organic materials
A column that does not continue down to the foundation
A column driven into the earth like a pile
questions.n: A planted column 'sits' on a beam or slab at an upper level rather than being aligned with the columns below.

questions.q: What is the result of 'Creep' in a concrete structure?
o: Long-term deformation under a constant load
Instant recovery after a load is removed
The growth of mold on the concrete
questions.n: Creep is the tendency of a solid material to move or deform permanently under the influence of persistent mechanical stresses.

questions.q: What is a 'Moment' in structural engineering?
o: The speed at which a load is applied
A measure of the tendency of a force to cause rotation
questions.n: A moment is the product of a force and its distance from a pivot point, creating a turning or bending effect.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of 'Post-tensioning' concrete?
o: It allows for longer spans and thinner slabs
It eliminates the need for any cement
It makes the concrete cheaper to buy
It makes the concrete look like wood
questions.n: By compressing the concrete after it hardens, post-tensioning counteracts tensile stresses, allowing for more efficient designs.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a 'Live Load'?
o: The weight of office furniture and equipment
The weight of the floor tiles
questions.n: Items that can be moved or changed during the building's life are classified as live loads.

questions.q: What does a 'Rebound Hammer' (Schmidt Hammer) test measure?
o: The surface hardness and estimated compressive strength
The moisture content of the soil
questions.n: The hammer measures the rebound of a spring-loaded mass, which correlates to the hardness and strength of the concrete surface.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of 'Shoring' in construction?
o: To mix the concrete on site
To provide temporary support for a structure during construction
questions.n: Shoring holds up slabs or beams while the concrete is still wet and has not yet reached its design strength.

questions.q: In structural steel, what does 'Yield Strength' indicate?
o: The stress level at which the steel starts to deform permanently
The maximum temperature the steel can handle
The weight of the steel beam
The point where the steel begins to rust
questions.n: Yield strength is the maximum stress a material can withstand before it no longer returns to its original shape.

questions.q: What is 'Modulus of Elasticity'?
o: The ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit
The total amount of steel in a beam
The time it takes for concrete to dry
The maximum weight a column can hold before buckling
questions.n: It measures a material's stiffness—how much it resists being stretched or compressed.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'Simply Supported Beam'?
o: A beam that is circular in shape
A beam that sticks out from a wall
A beam supported by a pin at one end and a roller at the other
A beam that is built into a wall at both ends
questions.n: Simply supported beams have supports at both ends that allow for rotation and some longitudinal movement.

questions.q: What is the function of a 'Purlin' in a roof structure?
o: To support the roof covering and transfer loads to the rafters
To provide insulation from the heat
To act as a drain for rainwater
questions.n: Purlins are horizontal members that sit on rafters or trusses to support the roofing sheets.

questions.q: What is 'Torsion' in a structural member?
o: The bending of a beam under a heavy load
The twisting of a member due to an applied torque
questions.n: Torsion occurs when forces try to rotate one part of a member relative to the rest.

questions.q: What is the primary risk of using 'Salt Water' in a concrete mix?
o: It makes the concrete set too slowly
It accelerates the corrosion of steel reinforcement
It makes the concrete turn blue
It makes the concrete taste bad
questions.n: Chlorides in salt water destroy the protective layer on steel rebars, leading to rapid rust and structural failure.

questions.q: What does 'F' followed by a number (e.g., F1, F2) usually signify on a foundation plan?
questions.n: The 'F' stands for footing, and the number refers to a specific size and reinforcement detail in the schedule.

questions.q: Which component of steel is primarily responsible for increasing its hardness but decreasing its ductility?
questions.n: Increasing carbon content enhances strength and hardness but makes the steel more brittle and less ductile.

questions.q: What is the primary cause of 'Differential Settlement' in a building's foundation?
o: Using the wrong type of cement
Uneven soil bearing capacity or non-uniform loading
questions.n: When different parts of a foundation settle by different amounts due to varying soil or loads, it causes structural stress.

questions.q: In a cantilever beam, where is the maximum tension reinforcement usually placed?
o: At the top of the beam
In the middle of the web
At the free end of the beam
At the bottom of the beam
questions.n: A cantilever beam bends downward, stretching the top fibers, thus requiring tension steel at the top.

questions.q: What is the standard ratio for a 'Class C' concrete mixture?
questions.n: Class C uses a 1:3:6 ratio and is generally used for non-structural elements like plant boxes or pathwalks.

questions.q: Which structural system relies primarily on the thickness of the walls to carry the weight of the building?
questions.n: A bearing wall system uses the walls themselves as the primary vertical load-carrying members.

questions.q: What is the term for the maximum stress a material can withstand before it breaks or fails completely?
questions.n: Ultimate strength is the maximum internal stress the material can reach on its stress-strain curve before rupture.

questions.q: Why is 'Potable Water' specified for mixing concrete?
o: To ensure no impurities interfere with the hydration process
To give the concrete a better color
To allow workers to drink from the same supply
To make the concrete safer to handle
questions.n: Potable water is free from acids, alkalis, and salts that could weaken the concrete or corrode reinforcement.

questions.q: What happens to a 'Short Column' when it fails under an axial load?
questions.n: Short columns have low slenderness and fail when the material's compressive strength is exceeded, leading to crushing.

questions.q: Which type of foundation is commonly used on sloping sites to maintain a level base for the structure?
questions.n: Stepped footings follow the slope of the ground in 'steps' to ensure the foundation remains level and stable.

questions.q: What is the primary role of 'Coarse Aggregate' in concrete?
o: To act as the binding agent
To fill the tiny voids between sand particles
To make the concrete easier to pump
To provide bulk and compressive strength to the mix
questions.n: Gravel or crushed stone (coarse aggregate) makes up the majority of the concrete volume and provides structural stability.

questions.q: What is 'Modulus of Rupture' a measure of?
questions.n: It measures the ability of a concrete beam or slab to resist failure in bending.

questions.q: In structural mechanics, what does the term 'Equilibrium' mean?
o: The point where a building collapses
When a beam is perfectly straight
The weight of the building equals the weight of the occupants
The state where all forces and moments cancel out to zero
questions.n: A structure is in equilibrium when the sum of all vertical, horizontal forces, and moments is zero, meaning it is not moving.

questions.q: What is the 'Neutral Axis' of a beam?
o: The most stressed part of the beam
The line where both tension and compression are zero
The top surface of the beam
The point where the beam is supported
questions.n: In a beam subjected to bending, the neutral axis is the layer that undergoes no change in length (no stress).

questions.q: Which of these is a major local supplier of cement in the Philippines?
questions.n: Holcim is one of the most prominent manufacturers of cement in the Philippines.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Shear Walls' in a high-rise building?
o: To provide a space for elevators
To resist lateral loads like wind and seismic forces
To act as a sound barrier between rooms
questions.n: Shear walls are stiff structural elements that prevent the building from swaying or 'racking' during earthquakes or high winds.

questions.q: What does 'PSI' stand for in concrete specifications?
questions.n: PSI is the imperial unit of pressure or stress used to measure concrete strength.

questions.q: What is 'Honeycombing' in a finished concrete column?
o: Surface voids where coarse aggregate is exposed without mortar
The pattern left by plywood forms
questions.n: Honeycombing is a defect caused by mortar failing to fill the spaces between aggregates, often due to poor vibration.

questions.q: What is a 'Moment-Resisting Frame'?
o: A frame that collapses in a moment
A frame where joints are rigid and resist rotation
A temporary frame used for photos
A frame that only carries dead loads
questions.n: In this system, the connections between beams and columns are stiff enough to transfer bending moments.

questions.q: In the context of the National Building Code, what is the 'Factor of Safety'?
o: The ratio of ultimate strength to allowable stress
The speed at which a building settles
The number of exits in a building
questions.n: It is a buffer used in design to ensure the building can handle more than the calculated load.

questions.q: What is the primary advantage of 'Pre-cast Concrete'?
o: Better quality control and faster on-site assembly
It is always cheaper than cast-in-place
It doesn't require any steel reinforcement
It weighs less than regular concrete
questions.n: Since members are made in a factory, conditions are controlled, and they can be installed quickly once they reach the site.

questions.q: What is 'Fatigue' in structural steel?
o: Failure due to repeated or cyclic loading
The melting of steel in a fire
The weight of the steel beam
When the steel gets tired and needs a break
questions.n: Fatigue occurs when a member is stressed and unstressed repeatedly, eventually leading to cracks and failure even at low stress levels.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'Grout' and 'Mortar'?
o: Grout is used for tiles, mortar is used for bricks
Mortar is only used for underground work
Grout is fluid and fills voids; mortar is thick and supports units
Grout has no cement in it
questions.n: Grout is a pourable mixture used to fill masonry cores, while mortar is a stiff paste used to bond blocks or bricks together.

questions.q: What is a 'Continuous Beam'?
o: A beam that is always pouring concrete
A beam made of a single piece of wood
A beam that spans across more than two supports
questions.n: Continuous beams span across three or more supports, which makes them more statically indeterminate and efficient.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is the standard length of a commercial reinforcing bar (rebar)?
questions.n: 6 meters is the standard length for rebars sold in the Philippines, though longer lengths can be ordered.

questions.q: Which structural member is designed to carry a load over an opening like a door or window?
questions.n: A lintel is a horizontal structural member (beam) that spans the opening between two vertical supports.

questions.q: What is 'Lateral Bracing'?
o: Members used to prevent buckling or sway from horizontal forces
questions.n: Lateral bracing provides stability against wind or seismic forces and prevents beams or columns from twisting.

questions.q: What is the primary function of the 'Neutral Axis' in a beam?
o: It is the region where stresses are zero during bending
To connect the beam to the column
To prevent the beam from rusting
questions.n: Because one side of a beam is in compression and the other in tension, there must be a 'neutral' layer in between.

questions.q: Which test is used to determine the bearing capacity of soil on site?
questions.n: A Plate Load Test determines the ultimate bearing capacity of soil and its probable settlement under load.

questions.q: What is 'Shear' stress?
o: Stress that causes parts of a body to slide past each other
Stress that pulls a material apart
questions.n: Shear stress acts parallel to a surface, trying to 'cut' or slide one section over another.

questions.q: What is the typical diameter for reinforcing bars in a standard 'Slab on Fill' for a house?
questions.n: 10 mm rebars are the standard size for temperature reinforcement in residential floor slabs.

questions.q: What is a 'Coffer Dam'?
o: A temporary watertight enclosure to allow construction under water
A permanent concrete wall to hold back soil
A dam made of coffee beans
questions.n: Coffer dams are used to pump water out of an area so foundations can be built on a dry riverbed or seabed.

questions.q: What is 'Buckling' of a column?
o: Sudden lateral bowing due to axial compression
questions.n: Buckling is an instability that occurs in slender members before the material's full strength is reached.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'Drip Mold' in a concrete slab or ledge?
o: To help the concrete set faster
To prevent rainwater from flowing back toward the wall
To provide a grip for workers
questions.n: A drip mold is a groove under a ledge that breaks the surface tension of water, forcing it to drop off.

questions.q: What is 'Pre-tensioning'?
o: Stretching tendons before the concrete is poured
Stretching tendons after the concrete has hardened
Mixing the concrete before the site is ready
Stretching the steel rebars until they break
questions.n: In pre-tensioning, steel tendons are stressed, then concrete is poured around them; once it hardens, the tension is released to compress the concrete.

questions.q: What is the result of 'Thermal Expansion' in a long steel bridge?
questions.n: Materials expand when heated, requiring expansion joints to prevent the structure from buckling or cracking.

questions.q: Which foundation type is essentially a very thick, large concrete slab that supports the entire building?
questions.n: A mat foundation acts as a single, massive slab that spreads the entire building load over the whole footprint.

questions.q: What is 'Deflection'?
o: The internal stress in a beam
The vertical displacement of a structural member under load
questions.n: Deflection is the 'sagging' or distance a beam moves from its original position when loaded.

questions.q: In the context of the National Building Code, what is a 'Space Frame'?
o: A 3D structural system of interconnected members
A frame built in outer space
A frame made of transparent glass
questions.n: Space frames are lightweight, rigid structures often used for large-span roofs like stadiums or hangars.

questions.q: What is 'Tension'?
o: A force that tries to stretch or pull a member apart
A force that tries to cut a member
A force that tries to twist a member
A force that tries to shorten a member
questions.n: Tension acts to elongate a structural component.

questions.q: Which type of stress is produced when a structural member is subjected to forces that tend to shorten it?
questions.n: Compression is the internal stress caused by external loads that push or squeeze the material together.

questions.q: In timber construction, what is the term for a beam that supports the ends of floor joists and transfers their loads to the columns?
questions.n: A girder is a large principal beam used to support smaller beams or joists.

questions.q: Which seismic wave is the fastest and usually the first to be recorded by a seismograph?
questions.n: Primary waves are longitudinal waves that travel the fastest through the Earth's interior.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of 'Diagonal Bracing' in a steel frame building?
o: To act as a fire-resistant barrier
To resist lateral loads and provide stiffness
questions.n: Diagonal members create stable triangles that resist horizontal forces from wind or earthquakes.

questions.q: What does the term 'Statistically Indeterminate' mean in structural engineering?
o: The structure is unstable and will collapse
The structure is only used for temporary construction
The structure cannot be solved using only the equations of equilibrium
questions.n: These structures have more reactions or internal forces than available equilibrium equations, requiring deformation analysis.

questions.q: In concrete work, what is 'Laitance'?
o: A specialized tool for leveling slabs
An admixture that speeds up curing
A weak, milky layer of cement and sand on the concrete surface
questions.n: Laitance is caused by bleeding water rising to the top, carrying fine particles that form a weak surface layer.

questions.q: What type of beam support allows for both rotation and horizontal movement but restricts vertical movement?
questions.n: Rollers allow the beam to expand or contract horizontally and rotate, while providing a vertical reaction.

questions.q: Which material is used in 'Gabion' walls for erosion control and retaining structures?
o: Stacked timber logs with steel pins
Rock or stones inside wire mesh cages
Interlocking plastic blocks filled with sand
questions.n: Gabions are modular cages filled with durable rocks, allowing for drainage and flexibility.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between a 'Live Load' and a 'Dead Load'?
o: Only dead loads are used in structural design
Dead loads are heavier than live loads
Dead loads are permanent; live loads are temporary and movable
questions.n: Dead loads come from the structure itself, while live loads include people, furniture, and environmental factors.

questions.q: In a simply supported beam with a point load at the center, where does the maximum shear force occur?
o: At the top fibers of the beam
questions.n: In a simply supported beam, the vertical reactions at the supports represent the maximum shear values.

questions.q: What is 'Camber' and why is it used in beams or trusses?
o: The width of the beam's flange
A downward curve to allow for drainage
The thickness of the protective paint on steel
An upward curvature provided to counteract future deflection
questions.n: By building an intentional upward curve, the beam will appear level once it sags under its design load.

questions.q: Which property of a soil indicates its ability to resist sliding and deformation under load?
questions.n: The shear strength of soil determines its bearing capacity and the stability of slopes.

questions.q: What is a 'Web Crippling' failure in a steel beam?
o: The snapping of the beam in half
The crushing or buckling of the web near a concentrated load or support
The twisting of the beam's flanges
The rusting of the middle section of the beam
questions.n: Excessive vertical pressure on the thin web can cause it to fold or buckle locally.

questions.q: In the Philippines, which government agency is responsible for issuing earthquake bulletins and volcanic warnings?
questions.n: The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology monitors geological phenomena.

questions.q: What is the function of a 'Shear Key' in a retaining wall?
o: To increase the compressive strength of the footing
To drain water from behind the wall
To prevent the wall from sliding horizontally
To provide a place to hang decorative panels
questions.n: A shear key is a projection below the base of the wall that 'bites' into the soil to increase resistance to sliding.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Base Isolation' in seismic design?
o: To glue the building to the ground as tightly as possible
To make the building taller without using more steel
To decouple the building from the ground motion
To prevent fire from spreading from the basement
questions.n: By using flexible bearings at the base, the ground can move while the building stays relatively still.

questions.q: In a structural steel drawing, what does the designation 'W14 x 90' mean?
o: A Wide Flange section approx. 14 inches deep weighing 90 lbs per foot
A wall 14 feet high with 90 windows
A beam 14 inches wide and 90 inches long
A welding specification for 14 to 90 mm steel
questions.n: W stands for Wide Flange; the first number is the nominal depth; the second is the linear weight.

questions.q: What is 'Creep' in timber members?
o: The sound wood makes when it is about to break
The way mold grows on wet lumber
Termite infestation spreading through the wood
Long-term deformation under a constant load, similar to concrete
questions.n: Timber will continue to sag over time if a constant load is applied, especially in humid conditions.

questions.q: Which foundation type is most suitable for a light structure built on very expansive (swelling) clay?
questions.n: These systems provide enough stiffness for the entire house to move as a single unit without cracking.

questions.q: What is 'Efflorescence' on a masonry wall?
o: A type of ivy that grows on old buildings
The process of the bricks turning into dust
White powdery salt deposits caused by moisture evaporation
questions.n: Water carries dissolved salts to the surface; when the water dries, the salt stays behind.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Fireproofing' steel columns in high-rise buildings?
o: To keep the steel from ever getting hot
To make the column look thicker and more imposing
To maintain structural strength long enough for evacuation
To prevent the steel from rusting
questions.n: Steel loses significant strength at high temperatures; fireproofing buys time before collapse.

questions.q: What is the primary benefit of a 'Fixed-End' beam compared to a 'Simply Supported' beam?
o: It has less deflection and can carry more load
questions.n: The rigid constraints at the ends resist rotation, making the beam stiffer and stronger.

questions.q: Which structural member connects two or more trusses together to provide lateral stability and support roofing?
questions.n: Purlins run horizontally across the rafters/trusses to distribute roof loads and tie the system together.

questions.q: What is a 'Cold Joint' in concrete construction?
o: An unintentional gap between two layers of concrete where the first has set
A joint filled with ice to keep the concrete cool
A joint specifically designed for snowy weather
A joint created by cutting with a diamond saw
questions.n: If new concrete is poured over old concrete that has already hardened, they may not bond properly.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is the 'Fire Code of the Philippines' also known as?
questions.n: Republic Act 9514 governs fire safety standards and inspections.

questions.q: What is the primary function of 'Ties' (Stirrups) in a reinforced concrete column?
o: To prevent the longitudinal bars from buckling outward
To increase the height of the column
To replace the need for cement
questions.n: Lateral ties provide confinement and keep the main vertical rebars in place under compression.

questions.q: What is 'Pre-stressing' concrete?
o: Worrying about the concrete before it arrives at the site
Applying an initial compressive stress to counteract future tension
Putting extra weight on the concrete while it's still wet
Using very old concrete that has been stressed for years
questions.n: By 'squeezing' the concrete with steel tendons, we can design members that handle much larger loads without cracking.

questions.q: Which type of floor system uses a series of closely spaced, small reinforced concrete beams?
questions.n: A ribbed slab uses small parallel beams (ribs) to provide strength while reducing the weight of the slab.

questions.q: What is the result of 'Scouring' around a bridge pier?
o: The pier expands due to heat
The pier becomes more resistant to earthquakes
The removal of soil from around the foundation by flowing water
questions.n: Scour can undermine a foundation, leading to settlement or collapse during a flood.

questions.q: What is the function of a 'Turnbuckle' in a cable or rod bracing system?
o: To connect the cable to the electricity grid
To act as a fuse that breaks during a fire
To adjust the tension in the rod or cable
To change the direction of the cable
questions.n: By rotating the turnbuckle, you can tighten or loosen the bracing to ensure it is taut.

questions.q: Which of these materials has the highest 'Strength-to-Weight' ratio?
questions.n: Steel is very strong, allowing for smaller, lighter members compared to concrete or masonry for the same load.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an 'Expansion Joint' in a very long building?
o: To act as a giant hinge for the building
To provide a location for the plumbing pipes
To allow for future extensions of the building
To allow the building parts to move independently due to temperature
questions.n: Long buildings can crack if they expand and contract as one giant piece; joints relieve this stress.

questions.q: What is the 'Slump' in a concrete slump test?
o: The vertical distance the concrete settles after the cone is removed
The time it takes for the concrete to dry
The amount of air trapped in the concrete
questions.n: Slump measures the 'wetness' and workability of the fresh concrete.

questions.q: In structural engineering, what is 'Resonance'?
o: The way light reflects off a glass facade
The sound a building makes during wind
The thickness of the wall for sound insulation
When the frequency of an external force matches the natural frequency of the structure
questions.n: Resonance can lead to massive, destructive vibrations, such as in the Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse.

questions.q: What is the function of 'Stiffeners' on a steel plate girder?
o: To make the beam easier to paint
To provide a place to attach electrical wires
To add extra weight for stability
To prevent the thin web from buckling locally
questions.n: They reinforce the vertical web plate against shear buckling and concentrated loads.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a 'Box Girder'?
o: A hollow, rectangular or trapezoidal structural section
A beam made of recycled cardboard boxes
A girder used to support storage boxes
A girder shaped like a triangle
questions.n: Box girders have excellent torsional (twisting) resistance and are common in bridge construction.

questions.q: What does 'Hydration' mean in the context of concrete curing?
o: Spraying the concrete with a hose to keep it wet
Drinking water at the job site
The evaporation of excess water from the surface
The chemical reaction between cement and water that hardens the mix
questions.n: Concrete doesn't 'dry' by evaporation; it hardens through a chemical bond with water.

questions.q: What is the primary role of the 'Flange' in an I-beam or Wide Flange section?
o: To resist the majority of the bending moment
To provide a surface for bird nests
To connect the beam to the flooring
questions.n: By placing mass far from the neutral axis, the flanges efficiently handle the tension and compression from bending.

questions.q: Which foundation type is most often used to support a heavy perimeter wall on a narrow property line?
questions.n: A strap footing connects an eccentric exterior footing to an interior one to prevent it from tipping over.

questions.q: What is 'Seismic Base Shear'?
o: The total lateral force at the base of a structure during an earthquake
The sound of the ground cracking
The total weight of the building's basement
The thickness of the shear walls
questions.n: Engineers calculate this force to determine how strong the foundation and structure must be to resist shaking.

questions.q: In timber design, what does 'Seasoning' refer to?
o: The time of year when the wood was cut
The natural pattern of the wood grain
Adding spices to the wood to prevent insects
Controlled drying of lumber to reduce moisture content
questions.n: Seasoned wood is stronger, more stable, and less likely to warp or shrink.

questions.q: What is a 'Moment of Inertia' a measure of?
o: How fast a beam falls down
The time a beam stays in place during an earthquake
The weight of the beam per meter
The resistance of a shape to bending based on its geometry
questions.n: A deeper beam has a higher moment of inertia and is much harder to bend than a flat, shallow one.

questions.q: What is the primary danger of 'Soft Story' buildings during an earthquake?
o: The building is located on soft, sandy soil
The roof is made of soft materials
A floor is significantly less stiff than the ones above it, leading to collapse
The paint on the walls is too soft
questions.n: This often happens in buildings with open parking on the ground floor and solid walls above.

questions.q: In structural steel, what is the 'Yield Point'?
o: The location where two beams meet
The point where the steel breaks
The temperature at which steel melts
The stress level where permanent deformation begins
questions.n: Before this point, the steel will spring back to its original shape; after this point, it stays bent.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Web' holes or openings in a steel beam?
o: To give workers a place to step
To allow for the passage of pipes and conduits
To let the air flow through the building
questions.n: Openings must be carefully placed and reinforced to avoid weakening the beam's shear capacity.

questions.q: What is 'Spalling' of concrete?
o: Mixing the concrete with a shovel
The chipping or flaking of the concrete surface
The process of pouring concrete into forms
The act of leveling the concrete
questions.n: Spalling is often caused by rusting rebars expanding inside the concrete or by freeze-thaw cycles.

questions.q: Which structural member is used to transfer loads from the roof to the walls or columns in a simple house?
questions.n: The top plate sits on the wall studs and provides a level surface for the rafters or trusses to rest on.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a 'Tied Arch' (Bowstring Arch)?
o: To prevent the arch ends from spreading outward
To support the heavy weight of the bridge floor
To provide a place for pedestrians to walk
To make the arch look like a bow and arrow
questions.n: The 'tie' (a tension member) holds the two ends together, allowing the arch to be used without massive abutments.

questions.q: In the Philippines, which local cement brand is often associated with the phrase 'Ibang Klaseng Galing'?
questions.n: This is a well-known advertising slogan for Republic Cement.

questions.q: What structural feature involves thickening or deepening a beam's section specifically to increase its moment resistance at a support?
questions.n: Increasing the depth of a beam near the supports efficiently manages higher negative moments.

questions.q: In structural analysis, a net resultant of shear forces acting vertically upward on the left side of a section is termed:
questions.n: By standard sign convention, upward forces on the left part of a sectioned beam indicate positive shear.

questions.q: Which type of foundation is specifically designed to accommodate a sloping site by changing levels in distinct stages?
questions.n: This method allows the foundation to follow the natural grade of a hill while keeping the base horizontal.

questions.q: What do you call the hard, pointed or rounded foot of a pile or caisson designed to pierce through underlying soil?
questions.n: The pile shoe protects the tip during driving and helps the pile penetrate harder soil layers.

questions.q: A rigid frame consisting of two columns and a beam defining a single bay is also known as a:
questions.n: In structural terminology, a bent is a transverse frame that provides lateral and vertical support.

questions.q: The horizontal movement of one level of a structure relative to the level immediately above or below it is called:
questions.n: Storey drift is the specific lateral displacement between adjacent floors during a seismic or wind event.

questions.q: What is the term for the maximum tensile, compressive, or shearing stress a material can bear without rupturing?
questions.n: Ultimate strength represents the peak stress on the stress-strain curve just before failure.

questions.q: Which property of fresh concrete is measured by the amount of useful internal work required to fully compact it?
questions.n: Workability encompasses the ease with which concrete can be mixed, placed, and compacted without segregation.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a rod placed between purlins to maintain their alignment and prevent sagging or twisting?
questions.n: Also known as sag rods, these ensure purlins remain properly spaced and aligned under load.

questions.q: A column that is not continuous to the foundation and instead rests on a beam or slab at an upper level is a:
questions.n: Planted columns are common in multi-use buildings where layout changes require shifting load paths.

questions.q: Which type of wood column consists of a single piece of timber, square or rectangular in cross-section?
questions.n: A solid column is the most basic form of timber support, consisting of one unified piece.

questions.q: What part of a structural steel 'Wide Flange' (W-shape) section connects the two flanges and resists shear?
questions.n: The web is the vertical plate that handles the majority of the shear forces in a beam.

questions.q: When a beam is stressed within its elastic limit, what occurs when the applied load is removed?
o: Beam will come back to its original state
questions.n: Elasticity is the property that allows a material to recover its shape once the stress is released.

questions.q: The theoretical maximum axial load a column can carry without buckling is known as the:
questions.n: Also known as the Euler load, it is the threshold where a column loses its stability.

questions.q: A column that fails by crushing rather than buckling because of its low height-to-width ratio is classified as a:
questions.n: Short columns are limited by material strength (crushing) rather than geometric instability (buckling).

questions.q: What does the 'Slenderness Ratio' of a column help structural engineers determine?
questions.n: The slenderness ratio is the primary indicator of whether a column will fail by buckling or crushing.

questions.q: Which deformation is most characteristic of a beam subjected to vertical loading?
questions.n: Deflection is the vertical displacement of a beam's neutral axis under load.

questions.q: What is the method of prestressing concrete where tendons are tensioned after the concrete has reached a certain strength?
questions.n: Tendons are placed in ducts and stressed after the concrete has hardened to apply compressive force.

questions.q: Which specific element of steel composition is most responsible for dictating its ductility?
questions.n: Higher carbon content increases hardness and strength but significantly reduces the steel's ductility.

questions.q: A structural system that does not have a complete vertical load-carrying space frame is often called a:
questions.n: In this system, walls serve as the primary support for vertical loads instead of a separate frame of columns.

questions.q: In a seismic event, which structural phenomenon occurs when the soil temporarily loses its strength and behaves like a viscous liquid?
questions.n: This occurs in saturated, loose, sandy soils where earthquake vibrations increase pore water pressure, causing the soil to lose shear strength.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a 'Grade Beam' in a foundation system?
o: To support walls and transfer loads to isolated footings or piles
To act as a primary decorative element of the base
To provide a level surface for floor tiling
To increase the compressive strength of the column
questions.n: Grade beams act as horizontal ties and load distributors, especially when soil conditions vary across the site.

questions.q: Which type of stress is dominant in a bolt used to connect two overlapping steel plates that are being pulled in opposite directions?
questions.n: The force acts parallel to the cross-section of the bolt, tending to 'cut' it across the plane where the plates meet.

questions.q: What is the recommended maximum spacing for lateral ties in a reinforced concrete column according to standard codes?
o: 16 times the diameter of the longitudinal bars
48 times the diameter of the tie bar
The largest dimension of the column
questions.n: This is a standard empirical rule to ensure longitudinal bars are sufficiently braced against buckling.

questions.q: In the design of a beach house, what is the most critical structural consideration for the roof system regarding wind loads?
questions.n: High-velocity winds creates a vacuum effect on leeward sides or over the roof, threatening to rip the structure upward.

questions.q: What structural effect occurs when the center of mass of a building does not coincide with its center of rigidity?
questions.n: The eccentricity between these two points causes the building to twist when subjected to lateral forces like wind or earthquakes.

questions.q: Which type of steel section is specifically designed to work as a 'tension member' in a truss, often using a threaded end for adjustment?
questions.n: Tie rods are slender members designed specifically to resist tension and are often adjustable to ensure proper alignment.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between a 'Bored Pile' and a 'Driven Pile'?
o: Bored piles are cast-in-place; driven piles are pre-fabricated
Driven piles are only made of wood
Bored piles cannot support heavy buildings
questions.n: Bored piles involve drilling a hole first, while driven piles are hammered into the ground as a finished unit.

questions.q: In a reinforced concrete beam, what happens to the 'Neutral Axis' as the applied bending moment increases and cracks form in the tension zone?
o: It shifts downward toward the steel
It remains exactly in the geometric center
It shifts upward toward the compression zone
questions.n: As tension concrete cracks, it no longer contributes, forcing the internal equilibrium to move the neutral axis higher.

questions.q: Which additive is most useful for concrete poured in a coastal environment to protect the reinforcement from salt-air intrusion?
questions.n: These chemicals form a protective film on the rebar or reduce the permeability of the concrete to chlorides.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Web Stiffeners' in a steel plate girder?
o: To increase the tensile strength of the flanges
To prevent the web from buckling under concentrated loads
To make the steel more resistant to rust
To reduce the overall weight of the beam
questions.n: The thin web of a girder is susceptible to local buckling, which these plates prevent by providing lateral support.

questions.q: What is 'Modulus of Resilience'?
o: The ability of a material to resist surface indentation
The ratio of stress to strain in the plastic range
The energy a material can absorb without permanent deformation
The total energy absorbed before the material ruptures
questions.n: It represents the area under the elastic portion of the stress-strain curve.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is the standard minimum width for a wall footing supporting a single-story hollow block wall?
questions.n: This is a common minimum width to ensure the load of a standard masonry wall is distributed to the soil.

questions.q: A 'Vierendeel Truss' is unique because it lacks which characteristic element of a standard truss?
questions.n: Unlike triangles in standard trusses, it uses rectangular openings and rigid joints to transfer loads.

questions.q: Which seismic wave causes the most damage to building foundations because of its rolling, elliptical motion?
questions.n: As a surface wave, it moves the ground both vertically and horizontally in a rolling motion, causing heavy structural stress.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of 'Shear Studs' (connector bolts) in a composite steel and concrete floor system?
o: To provide a mounting point for ceiling hangers
To ensure the steel beam and concrete slab act as a single unit
To increase the fire rating of the steel
questions.n: They prevent the slab from sliding over the beam, allowing them to share the bending stresses.

questions.q: In structural drawing, what does 'O.C.' stand for, especially regarding rebar or joist spacing?
questions.n: This indicates that the measurement is taken from the center of one member to the center of the next.

questions.q: What is 'Pascal' (Pa) a unit of in the SI system?
questions.n:
One Pascal is equal to one Newton per square meter (

questions.q: Which factor in the 'Water-Cement Ratio' is most responsible for the presence of capillary pores in hardened concrete?
o: Excess water not used for hydration
questions.n: Water that does not chemically react with cement eventually evaporates, leaving microscopic voids.

questions.q: In the Philippines, which code specifically governs the design of wood structures?
o: NSCP (National Structural Code of the Philippines)
questions.n: Chapter 6 of the NSCP specifically details the standards and allowable stresses for timber design.

questions.q: In a seismic analysis of a building, what is the 'Period of Vibration'?
o: The maximum velocity reached by the building during ground shaking
The time required for a structure to complete one full cycle of motion
The frequency at which the building vibrates per second
The total duration of the earthquake event in seconds
questions.n: This definition correctly describes the fundamental period, which is influenced by the building's mass and stiffness.

questions.q: What is the primary reason for placing 'Shear Stirrups' closer together near the supports of a simply supported beam?
o: Because bending moment is highest at the supports
To counteract the maximum shear force occurring at the supports
To prevent the longitudinal bars from rusting
To increase the compressive strength of the concrete
questions.n: Shear force is typically greatest at the support locations, requiring more reinforcement to prevent diagonal tension failure.

questions.q: Which type of stress is characterized by a 'pulling' force that acts to elongate a structural member?
questions.n: Tension occurs when forces act away from each other along the same axis, stretching the material.

questions.q: According to the National Structural Code of the Philippines (NSCP), what is the minimum concrete cover for rebars in beams NOT exposed to weather or in contact with the ground?
questions.n: Standard code requirements specify this depth for beams and columns to ensure fire rating and durability in non-exposed conditions.

questions.q: What does 'Poisson's Ratio' represent in material science?
o: The ratio of weight to volume
The ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
The ratio of ultimate strength to yield strength
The ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit
questions.n: This ratio describes how a material thins out when stretched or widens when compressed.

questions.q: Which structural system is most effective at resisting lateral loads in high-rise buildings by utilizing the rigid outer perimeter?
questions.n: By spacing exterior columns closely, the entire building acts like a giant cantilevered pipe to resist wind and seismic forces.

questions.q: In timber design, what is 'Check' as a physical defect?
o: A hole left by a fallen branch
A longitudinal crack across the growth rings
questions.n: Checking is a seasoning defect caused by uneven drying, resulting in cracks that do not usually go through the entire thickness.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a 'Turnbuckle' in a steel bracing system?
o: To connect a beam to a column rigidly
To increase the shear capacity of a bolt
To adjust the tension in tie rods or cables
To provide fire protection to the steel
questions.n: The threaded mechanism allows for precise tightening of bracing to ensure the frame is plumb and stable.

questions.q: What happens to the 'Neutral Axis' of a beam when it is subjected to pure bending?
o: It disappears if the load is too heavy
It remains unstressed and its length does not change
questions.n: By definition, the neutral axis is the boundary between compression and tension where stress is zero.

questions.q: In a traverse calculation for surveying, what is the 'Departure' of a line?
o: The vertical distance or change in Northing
The total length of the line measured on the ground
The horizontal distance or change in Easting
The angle measured from the North-South meridian
questions.n: Departure represents the X-axis component of a line's vector, moving East or West.
